*from Pia Arke's exhibition* Arctic Hysteria *at Greenland's National Museum & Archives, Nuuk, 2010*

**i.**
I dwell within my body. I am here, before you. I am the very temperature of this room. I stand disrobed in my nakedness; I am the light and shadow that you feel. I resemble other people more than I resemble you. I possess a before and an after. I am my self, wholly and solely. My exterior and interior flow as one. I am muscle, organ, fluid, and bone. I am monumental. You alone are the one who sees me.

**ii.**
I am not naked as I truly am; I am naked as you behold me. I am transparent, almost visible. I belong to a time and a place. I am tribal and exotic. I am forever compelled to bear objects. You are heroic. I am an entire museum, the chronicle of my own making. I am a mirror held up to you; you are reflected in the very act of looking upon me. At best, I mimic you. You author me. When you depart, I shall cease to exist.

**iii.**
I am a single point of consciousness. I am indifferent. I am unself, like a photogram. I am prehistoric, existing before all definition. Your body descends upon me. I possess depth and luminescence. I am neither here nor there; I extend infinitely. I dwell within the lived world, the light and darkness within my head like the very substance of dreams. I am the camera obscura, the room itself. I both adore and resist.

From Pia Arke's *Arctic Hysteria* exhibition, presented at Greenland's National Museum & Archives in Nuuk, 2010

**i.**
My body contains me. Right here, I stand before your gaze. The warmth filling this space is mine. Stripped bare in my nakedness, I become both the brightness and the shadow that touches you. To all others I bear resemblance—it is only to you that I am foreign. A past trails me, and a future waits ahead. Wholly and exclusively, I belong to myself. There is no break between what lies within me and what shows without. Sinew, tissue, liquid, and skeleton compose me. My presence towers. Yours are the only eyes upon me.

**ii.**
What you witness is not my true nakedness but the nakedness you construct. I turn see-through, hovering at the edge of sight. A moment holds me, a location fixes me. To you I seem primitive and strange. Forever I am made to hold up artifacts. The hero's role falls to you. I am an entire collection, the record of my own fashioning. In me you find your reflection; gazing upon me, you glimpse yourself. If I succeed, it is only in copying you. Your hand authors my existence. The instant you depart, I dissolve into nothing.

**iii.**
I narrow to one aware speck. Nothing stirs me. I am selfless, like an imprint of light on paper. I belong to a time before names, before meaning took shape. Your form descends across mine. Within me lies depth and a faint inner glow. Neither present nor absent, I stretch out without limit. My dwelling is the world as it is felt, the brightness and murk within my skull as insubstantial as a dream. I am the darkened chamber, the very room. In me, longing and defiance live together.

# On the Body Seen and the Body Owned

## I. The Self-Defined Body

In the opening movement, the speaker asserts an identity forged entirely from within. Here, the body is not fragmented or partial but unified—a single, continuous form that admits no separation between its inner life and its outer presentation. It stands monumental, possessing the solidity and permanence of something carved rather than merely fleshed. What one is inside and what one presents outside are not two truths in tension but one truth flowing seamlessly through the whole. This is the body as self-possession: whole, sovereign, and unbroken, claiming its own meaning before any other voice can intervene.

## II. The Body Constructed by the Gaze

The second movement disrupts this sovereignty. Here, identity is no longer self-generated but assembled from the outside—built, shaped, and held in place by an external observer. The speaker exists only insofar as the observer sees them, writes them into being, and reflects their image back. Selfhood becomes contingent, a projection sustained by another's attention. When the gaze looks away, the question lingers: does anything remain? This section reveals the vulnerability of a self that has been outsourced, an identity that survives only in the observer's perception and testimony.

## III. The Tension Between Possession and Objectification

At the heart of the work lies the friction between these two modes of being—the body that owns itself and the body that is owned by the eyes upon it. This tension crystallizes through the motifs of nudity, exoticization, and spectacle. The unclothed body, which might signify honesty or freedom, is instead rendered into an object of display. The speaker is exoticized—made strange, made "tribal," transformed into a curiosity to be catalogued and admired from a distance. Like an artifact behind museum glass, the self is preserved and presented, but at the cost of its living agency. Authenticity and objectification here are not opposites but uncomfortable neighbors, each shadowing the other.

## IV. The Dissolved Consciousness

The third movement releases the tension into abstraction. Consciousness loosens its grip on any fixed location, ceasing to reside solely in the bounded, monumental body of the first section. Instead, it disperses and merges with the surrounding space, becoming the very room that receives light and image. The speaker turns into a camera obscura—a darkened chamber through which the outer world is projected, inverted, and held. No longer simply the thing observed, the self becomes the apparatus of observation, the space in which seeing itself occurs. This is a transcendence of the earlier binaries: neither wholly subject nor object, but the medium through which images pass.

## Conclusion

Across all three movements, the work sustains an interrogation of the bond between the observed and the observer. It refuses to resolve neatly on either side. The speaker is caught in ambivalence—simultaneously adoring the external forces that grant them shape and definition, and resisting the way those same forces reduce, contain, and possess them. In the end, the text does not choose between self-possession and surrender; it holds both, insisting that to be seen is at once to be created and to be claimed, to be honored and to be taken.

# The Body Between Self and Spectacle: Pia Arke's *Arctic Hysteria*

Pia Arke's poetic text, created for her *Arctic Hysteria* exhibition, is a meditation on one of the most fraught experiences of the colonized subject: the sensation of being watched, measured, and defined by eyes that are not one's own. At its core, the work explores the tension between self-perception and external objectification—the gap that opens between how we understand ourselves from within and how we are constructed by the gaze of others. This is not an abstract philosophical exercise. For Arke, whose own Greenlandic and Danish heritage placed her at the intersection of colonizer and colonized, the question of who holds the authority to see, name, and interpret a body carries profound personal and political weight.

## Three Shifting Perspectives

The text achieves its interrogative force through a structure of three shifting perspectives. Rather than presenting a single, stable voice, Arke moves between vantage points, refusing to let the reader settle into a comfortable position of observation. This restlessness is deliberate. By moving between the one who sees, the one who is seen, and perhaps the uneasy space between them, the text enacts the very dislocation it describes. The reader is made to feel what it means to be caught in a system of looking—to be simultaneously subject and object, observer and observed.

These shifting perspectives allow Arke to ask a persistent and uncomfortable question: how are bodies seen, defined, and constructed by others? The exoticized or colonized body, in particular, rarely exists on its own terms. It is written into being through the interpretations of outsiders—ethnographers, photographers, tourists, and administrators—who arrive with their categories already prepared. The body becomes a surface onto which meanings are projected, its own testimony overwritten by the authoritative accounts of those who claim the right to describe it.

## Selfhood Between Autonomy and Imposition

What emerges from this movement is a portrait of identity in a state of oscillation. The text reveals how selfhood is never fixed but continually swings between two poles: on one side, an autonomous sense of being—the self that knows itself from the inside, that possesses interiority, memory, and desire; on the other, the imposed roles handed down by external forces. Chief among these imposed roles are those of spectacle and mirror.

To be made a spectacle is to be reduced to something looked at, a curiosity or object of fascination stripped of subjectivity. To be made a mirror is perhaps even more insidious: it is to be emptied of one's own content so that the observer might see only a reflection of their own assumptions, fantasies, and fears. In both cases, the observed subject loses the ability to define herself. Arke's text captures the vertigo of living within this oscillation, never allowed to rest securely in one's own selfhood, always at risk of being pulled back into the roles that others have prepared.

## Critiquing the Colonial and Ethnographic Gaze

Ultimately, the work delivers a powerful critique of the colonial and ethnographic gaze. This gaze operates with a peculiar and violent doubleness: it both writes and erases the subject it observes. It writes the subject by producing endless descriptions, classifications, images, and reports—an entire apparatus of knowledge that claims to capture the truth of the observed body. Yet in the same gesture, it erases that subject, replacing her living reality with a constructed image that serves the purposes of the observer. The person disappears beneath the representation.

By exposing this dynamic, Arke does more than describe an injustice; she reclaims a measure of agency. In naming the mechanisms of the gaze, in making the reader feel their disorienting effects, she interrupts the seamless authority of colonial and ethnographic looking. *Arctic Hysteria* thus stands as both a lament and an act of resistance—a work that insists on the irreducible interiority of the observed subject, even as it lays bare the forces that would reduce her to spectacle and mirror.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic three-part meditation in the voice of Pia Arke's body/photographic self, inspired by her exhibition "Arctic Hysteria" at Greenland's National Museum, exploring themes of nudity, the colonial gaze, and the camera obscura.
counterfactuals.output:
# Three Meditations in the Voice of the Body-Camera

*after Pia Arke*

---

## I. The Body as Darkroom

I am the box that holds the light,
the pinhole through which country enters me—
inverted, trembling, upside down.

They built me long, a coffin-length of wood,
a body I must climb inside to see.
Here in the dark I am both lens and land,

both the seer and the thing being seen.
Naked, I lie against the photographic paper,
pressing my Greenland-flesh to silver,

and the sun comes slow through the small wound
I have opened in the black.
It takes an hour. It takes my patience.

I develop as the ice develops:
by exposure, by the long endurance
of standing still beneath the gaze.

---

## II. The Colonial Eye

You measured me before you named me.
You wrote *hysteria* across the tundra of my skin
as though the cold could make a woman mad,

as though my dancing, my refusals, my dark laughter
were a disease you could photograph and file
in the museums of your certainty.

I know the arithmetic of your looking:
the calipers, the plates, the naked women
lined against the wall like specimens of weather.

So I return your stare. I take the camera
you turned on my grandmothers
and I turn it back—but softer, slower,

letting the light take its own long time
to write me into being. I am not your data.
I am the one who now decides the exposure.

---

## III. The Long Undressing

To be naked here is not to be undone.
I lie against the paper and I let
the pinhole map me with its single eye—

no photographer, no witness but the sun,
no hand but mine that opened up the dark.
This is the nudity of reclamation:

I am the model and the maker both,
the flesh and the machine that renders flesh,
the coast redrawn by its own longing.

See how the landscape prints across my belly,
how ice and body blur their boundaries,
how *place* and *person* are the same slow bloom.

I am half-Danish, half-Greenlandic, wholly here—
a camera obscura walking on two legs,
turning the whole world upside down to see it true.

---

*Note: Pia Arke (1958–2007) was a Greenlandic-Danish artist whose work "Arctic Hysteria" confronted colonial anthropology, ethnographic photography, and questions of hybrid identity. She famously constructed a body-sized pinhole camera and used the camera obscura as both method and metaphor.*

# Specimen / Self-Portrait

I am the temperature of a room someone else set. I am the humidity they maintain to keep me from cracking.

*

I am salt in the crease of my own elbow. You are the placard that says *origin unknown.*

I am the sound my knees make in the morning. You are the caption: *note the graceful curvature.*

*

They photographed me against a cloth the color of no country. I am the country. I am also the cloth, folded away when the shooting stops.

*

I am hunger at 2 p.m. I am the particular way I hold a spoon. You framed the hand and called it *ancestral gesture.* I was only reaching for soup.

*

Under glass I am cooler than I feel. The light is calibrated to flatter what it isn't warming. I am behind the reflection of your face, so that when you look you see us both and call the composite *me.*

*

I am the wet interior of a yawn.
You are the description: *the subject appears at rest.*

I am the itch I cannot reach on my own back.
You are the arrow pointing to the scar, the little essay beneath it.

*

Somewhere there is a drawer of me. Index cards. A number where a mouth should be. I am filed under *representative example.* I am asked to represent. I did not agree to stand for the others, but the frame is wide and I am inside it.

*

I am the breath I take before the shutter.
The shutter takes the breath.
Now I am the held one, the still one, the *timeless,* which only means: not permitted to age, not permitted to leave.

*

Listen— I am the sweat you edited out.
I am the blink you waited past.
I am the boredom of standing exactly here so the composition holds.

*

You will hang me where the light is best.
I will go on being the temperature of a room I did not set,
salt in the crease of my own arm,
reaching, still, for soup.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a text response to Pia Arke's work that engages with ideas of the camera obscura, postcolonial Greenlandic identity, and the relationship between subject and observer, structured in three numbered sections.
counterfactuals.output:
# Response to Pia Arke: Chambers of Seeing

## 1. The Camera Obscura as Body and History

Pia Arke's construction of a camera obscura large enough to enter—her pinhole camera built to the scale of a body—transforms the optical instrument into a dwelling, a womb, a room of colonial reckoning. The camera obscura has always carried a double inheritance: it is both the Enlightenment's proud emblem of rational vision and the mechanism by which the world is captured, inverted, and made possess-able. To walk *inside* the apparatus, as Arke insisted on doing, is to refuse the position of the disembodied European eye that surveys the North from a comfortable distance.

There is an argument embedded in her method. Photography arrived in Greenland as an extension of the expedition, the survey, the ethnographic catalogue. The land and its people were fixed on plates before they were consulted. Arke's oversized apparatus slows this violence into visibility. Light bleeds through the aperture across long exposures, and the image forms not through instantaneous seizure but through duration, through waiting, through the photographer's own presence within the machinery of representation. The instrument that once objectified becomes, in her hands, a chamber where she is simultaneously the one who sees and the thing seen.

## 2. Postcolonial Greenlandic Identity and the Problem of the In-Between

Arke, born of a Greenlandic mother and a Danish father, worked from a position she named directly: the space of the person who belongs fully to neither category the colonial archive prepared. Her concept of "ethno-aesthetics"—a term she borrowed and turned ironic—refuses the neat separation of the anthropological object from the art-making subject. She asked what it means to be studied, sorted, and displayed by a nation that governs your land while claiming to protect it.

Her photographs of the Greenlandic landscape are not the sublime emptiness of the explorer's imagination. They are haunted, scratched, layered with her own scale-figure, insisting that this terrain is not virgin territory awaiting European description but a place already inhabited, already narrated, already loved. In works assembling family snapshots, official records, and historical documents, she stitches the personal into the political and exposes how identity in a colonized place is never simply given—it is negotiated against an archive that was built to define you from outside.

The strength of this position is its refusal of purity. Arke does not offer an authentic, pre-colonial Greenland to be recovered. She works instead within the contamination, using the coloniser's own instruments—the camera, the museum vitrine, the ethnographic method—against their original purpose.

## 3. Subject and Observer: The Collapse of Distance

At the center of Arke's practice lies a deliberate confusion of who observes whom. The classical relationship between observer and subject depends on distance and asymmetry: the observer is active, mobile, invisible; the subject is passive, fixed, exposed. Colonial photography perfected this asymmetry. Arke's entire project can be read as an effort to fold that distance back on itself.

When she places her own body inside the camera obscura, she occupies both poles at once. When she photographs herself against Greenlandic land, she is author and evidence, eye and specimen. This is not a resolution but a productive instability. It asks the viewer standing before her work to feel their own position destabilised—to notice that looking is never innocent, that the gaze carries a history of power, and that the person being looked at has always been looking back.

The final gift of Arke's work may be this reversal: she returns the stare. The North that was surveyed becomes a place from which we, the observers, are examined. In doing so she reclaims not only images but the very act of seeing—insisting that vision belongs to the one who was meant only to be seen.

---

*A note on engagement: Arke's power lies in her insistence that theory be embodied and located. Any response to her should resist the temptation to make her a mere illustration of postcolonial ideas—her contribution is that she lived the questions in the flesh, in the land, and inside the machine.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

# Three Movements for a Figure Behind Glass

## I. The Body Assembled

I am the shoulder turned away from you.
I am the hip that holds its weight in stillness.
I am the pulse you cannot see but know is there,
somewhere beneath the surface you keep watching.

I am assembled here from what I carry—
the ache of standing, the labor of remaining,
the small rebellion of a breath.

You are the eyes that finish what I start.
You are the distance that makes me visible.
You are the reason I have learned to hold a pose
as if a pose could be a kind of living.

---

## II. The Looking

I am watched, and watching makes me solid.
I am the object and the offering.
I am the surface where your gaze lands, softly,
then lingers longer than I gave permission.

You are the light that decides my edges.
You are the hunger that mistakes me for a window.
You are the one who leans in close, then closer,
believing nearness is the same as knowing.

I am not the thing you think you see.
I am the thing that sees you seeing me.
I am the shiver in the space between us,
the flicker where the watched begins to watch.

---

## III. The Fixed Image

I am flattened now, and framed, and finished.
I am the moment amputated from its minutes.
I am the light that fell on me one instant,
kept like an insect underneath the glass.

You are the future looking back at nothing.
You are the album, the archive, the museum.
You are the one who says *this is her,*
holding a paper ghost against your chest.

I am here and I am gone at once.
I am the body and the body's absence.
I am the promise photographs keep breaking:
that you could hold me still and call it *have.*

You are still looking.
I am still here.
We are the distance that will not close.

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine wall text or an artist statement for Pia Arke's "Arctic Hysteria" (Nuuk, 2010) that dramatizes the tension between self-possession and being made into an object of ethnographic display.
counterfactuals.output:
# Arctic Hysteria
## Pia Arke (1958–2007)

*Wall text, Nuuk, 2010*

---

Watch her crawl.

In the film that gives this work its name, the artist moves naked across a vast photograph of the Greenlandic landscape—her birthplace, her supposed origin, the terrain onto which an entire people has been projected as *nature*. She presses her body against the image. She tears it. She gathers the fragments beneath her.

Consider what you are being asked to do here: to look.

To look is the whole colonial apparatus in miniature. For more than a century, the Arctic and its inhabitants were photographed, measured, catalogued, and diagnosed. "Arctic hysteria"—*pibloktoq*—was a condition Western observers invented to name the supposed madness of the northern native, a woman especially, seized by fits, tearing off her clothes, fleeing across the ice. It was a disorder that existed chiefly in the observer's need to find one. The ethnographer named the madness; the madness confirmed the ethnographer.

Arke seizes the diagnosis and performs it back to us.

She was born of a Greenlandic mother and a Danish father—a body the colonial file could not cleanly categorize, standing between the one who looks and the one who is looked at. She trained the camera she was meant to sit before. She built her own pinhole cameras large enough to enter, turning the instrument of capture into a room she could inhabit. She read the archive against itself, asking who held the lens, who was permitted a name, who became merely a *type*.

Here is the tension she refuses to resolve:

To be seen is to be made. The landscape behind her is not memory but *representation*—someone else's Greenland, printed and pinned. When she crawls across it, is she reclaiming her ground or performing the very savagery the West wrote for her? Is she the subject possessing herself, or the object completing the fantasy of her own wildness?

She will not tell you.

She keeps both truths in her hands at once: the self that acts and the image that was acted upon; the woman who directs and the specimen who was displayed. She occupies the diagnosis so fully that it breaks open, and in the tearing—the destruction of the picture beneath her—she does the one thing the ethnographic gaze never permitted its object.

She looks back.

---

*Ethnography here becomes a mirror. The question the work leaves in the room is not "what is she," but "what are you doing when you watch."*
